as_told: Builders who dig mega-basements under rich London homes cannot drive the digger out of the deep hole. Lifting it out with a crane costs more than the digger is worth, so they bury it under gravel and concrete. Hundreds, perhaps 1,000, diggers are said to lie under west London.
lesson: In London's top property market the sums are so large that throwing away a working machine is cheaper than getting it out.
what_happened: The story was first printed by Ed Smith in the New Statesman on 5 June 2014. He gave no named source; he wrote that one developer he asked guessed at least 1,000 and another 500. The next day the Evening Standard quoted a director of the developer Galliard and the managing director of Cranbrook Basements, who called it ludicrous and said the small diggers can be lifted out with a block and tackle. No record of an actual buried digger under a London house was found.
false_part: No record shows any digger buried under a London basement; the only sources are two unnamed developers, and named basement builders deny it.

earliest_telling.where: The bizarre secret of London's buried diggers, New Statesman
earliest_telling.quote: One property developer I asked reckoned at least 1,000; another put the figure at more like 500.

original.what: Evening Standard, 6 June 2014: interview statement by Kevin O'Connor, managing director of Cranbrook Basements
original.quote: The diggers used are tiny little machines and they can be lifted out with a block and tackle. There is always an exit strategy for the equipment.

original.what: Evening Standard, 6 June 2014: interview statement by Don O'Sullivan, a director of the London developer Galliard
original.quote: why would someone leave such valuable space filled with dumped equipment and fill in concrete?

lesson_verdict.why: No cost record or study of basement building was found that compares the value of a small digger with the cost of lifting it out. The only named builders quoted say removal is cheap and that the basement space is worth far more than the machine.

source.what: Evening Standard, 6 June 2014: Don O'Sullivan of Galliard on the value of basement space
source.quote: With the basement space worth up to £8,000 per sq ft

search_steps: Web search for buried diggers under London basements: all tellings point to Ed Smith, New Statesman, 5 June 2014; the story spread the same week (Telegraph, ITV, Boing Boing, Gizmodo).
Saved the New Statesman article: the live page is cut off by a paywall; saved a full copy from the Wayback Machine (2020 snapshot).
Saved HuffPost UK (Charlotte Meredith, 6 June 2014) as a lead only; followed its link to the Evening Standard article of 6 June 2014.
The live Evening Standard page refused access (Cloudflare 403); saved the Wayback Machine copy of 6 June 2014.
Searched for an earlier telling (before June 2014) and for a documented case of a buried digger; found none.

Tried Kensington and Chelsea council basement studies (Alan Baxter, 2013 and 2014) for how plant is removed; the council site refused access (403); the 2014 case-study report from the Wayback Machine covers spoil and lorries, not diggers, so it was not used.
Rule 3: searched for a correction or reply by Ed Smith or the New Statesman; found none. The 2020 archived page carries no correction note.
Open Library and newspaper archives were not searched; the story is from 2014.
confidence_note: An earlier oral or forum version before June 2014 may exist but was not found. The builders' denials are interview statements in a newspaper, and they have a business interest. That no digger has ever been buried cannot be proven; the class rests on the lack of any record.
